turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Err, sorry, this screen's frozen again. Uh, right. What brings you in?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Good afternoon, doctor. Thank you for seeing me. I have had a blocked nose and a pressure across my face since a cold about ten days ago.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Blocked nose. Sorry, say that again? Ten days?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, doctor. The cold began about ten days ago. The sneezing has settled, but the nose is still blocked, and there is a green discharge.
[SEG0005] person_3 (CAREGIVER): And he's tired. This is the second week of it.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): That is correct, doctor. The tiredness has gone on for a fortnight.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Umm. The green discharge, both sides? And is it painful?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Both sides, I am afraid. It is not painful. It is a pressure, and it is worse when I bend forward.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. Any fever?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Not really. I did check at home this morning, though. It was thirty seven point four.
[SEG0011] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Mm. I saw the thermometer too. Thirty seven point four.
[SEG0012] person_1 (DOCTOR): Thirty seven point four. Hang on, still typing. Are you on a nose spray?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes. The Otrivin, from the chemist. Two sprays each side, every day.
[SEG0014] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry, two sprays? The cursor jumped.
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): Two sprays in each nostril, once a day, for these ten days.
[SEG0016] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He sleeps badly as well. I hear him up two or three times a night.
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): I am afraid that is true. My sleep has been poor these past weeks.
[SEG0018] person_1 (DOCTOR): Of. Let me open the history. High blood pressure is on the file. Is that still going?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes. I have had hypertension for five-ish years. I take the water tablet for it.
[SEG0020] person_1 (DOCTOR): Which water tablet? Uh, the dose is not on the screen.
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Indapamide. Two and a half milligrams, every morning.
[SEG0022] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Except he does not take the tablets on Sundays. The Sunday one is always still in the pack.
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Forgive me, that is not right. I miss Saturday, not Sunday.
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): Saturday. Not Sunday. Any chest pain?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): Breathlessness? With the blood pressure, I mean.
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Not really. Never, actually.
[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): And swelling of the ankles?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): No... well, sometimes. By the evening, if I have been on my feet.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sometimes. Sorry, I was on the wrong note. Say that once more?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Sometimes, doctor. In the evenings.
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any cough?
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sore throat?
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): Earache?
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Not that either.
[SEG0038] person_3 (CAREGIVER): There was a cut on his hand, from the secateurs. It healed in five days.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Was that slow to heal?
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): No, doctor. It healed quite normally, in five days.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good. Any allergies to medicines? Penicillin or anything?
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): No. None that I know of.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll have a look. The nose is blocked, there is green mucus, and the forehead is tender over the sinuses. Chest is clear.
[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): Blood pressure is one forty two over eighty eight. Pulse is seventy four. Sorry, did you catch that?
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): One forty two over eighty eight, and seventy four. Thank you.

[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): This is most likely a sinus infection after the cold. Most of them settle without antibiotics. I'll write a back-up script for amoxacillin, five hundred milligrams by mouth three times a day for 5 days. Do not start it unless you are no better in three days, or you get a proper fever.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): I understand. Should I continue the Otrivin?

[SEG0048] person_1 (DOCTOR): Stop the Otrivin, it will only block the nose more. Saline washes are fine. If you're no better in a week, come back and see me. Sooner if an eye swells or the pain turns severe.

spec.situation: Blocked nose, facial pressure and green discharge ten days after a cold; second week of tiredness; uses nasal spray daily; doctor explains most settle without antibiotics, gives a back-up plan.

traps.happens: A caregiver or relative reports observations ('the cut healed in five days', 'she sleeps badly', 'he does not take the tablets on Sundays'); the patient agrees, disagrees or corrects one point. The nurse also reports a measurement that the patient mentioned before.
traps.label_rule: reported_by follows who said it. A healing cut that healed normally is a negative finding (no slow-healing wounds) or nothing, NOT a symptom. A disputed fact is recorded with certainty disputed or as an uncertainty. A correction replaces the earlier value (Saturday, not Sunday).

traps.happens: The patient denies some symptoms (said as 'no', 'not really', 'never'), has a chronic condition named earlier (for example asthma or hypertension) and later the doctor asks about another symptom of it, and one answer is a double negative or a correction ('not that either', 'no... well, sometimes').
traps.label_rule: Denials go in negative_findings with the exact thing denied, never in symptoms. NEVER write a negative about a condition the patient has said they have. A corrected answer keeps only the final version. A negative is never a symptom, and 'not painful' is the finding 'pain' absent, not a symptom called 'painless'.

features: spoken_numbers: doses, vitals and durations are spoken as words or sloppy speech ('a hundred and two point five', 'one-forty over ninety', 'five-ish years', 'twenty milligram'); the label writes them normally (102.5, 140/90, 20 mg) and does not turn vague ones into exact ones.

colloquial_drug_names: medicines referred to by colour, purpose or brand ('the water tablet', 'Crocin', 'my sugar tablets', 'the purple inhaler'); the name is recorded as said, the normalized name only if it is clear.
spec.doctor_style: distracted by the computer, asks for repeats
